description: Earth is our most accessible laboratory for preparing to explore the Moon and Mars. Scientists and engineers already use terrestrial “analog” environments — deserts, polar regions, volcanic landscapes, impact craters, and caves — to study planetary processes and test instruments, technologies, and exploration concepts. However, no location on Earth perfectly reproduces another planetary environment, and different locations may provide useful analogs for different characteristics.
summary:
ALSTRO-Y: Earth Analogs for the Moon and Mars
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Al-Karak, Jordan

Astronauts must train on Earth before working on the Moon or Mars, where communication delays force crews to solve problems alone. We used NASA data to find the best Earth matches for two NASA targets.

Results

	•	Shackleton Crater (Moon, south pole) ↔ Haughton Crater, Canada: 66% similarity. Both are impact craters of similar size (21 and 23 km), with ground ice and polar light.
	•	Jezero Crater (Mars) ↔ Wadi Rum, Jordan: 74% similarity. Iron-rich red sand, sandstone and dry valleys carved by ancient water.

A cross-check shows that each Earth site matches its own target best (Haughton–Jezero 52%, Wadi Rum–Shackleton 36%).

Method
We scored each pair on eight weighted dimensions. Three of them (light, temperature, dryness) are calculated automatically by our Python code from live NASA POWER data. The team rated the other five from published research. We also used MODIS, ASTER, Worldview, Moon Trek and Mars Trek.

What NASA gains: safer, cheaper training, rover testing in Mars-like terrain, and a scoring tool that can be used again.

Limitations: no place on Earth has low gravity, vacuum or space radiation.

Deliverables: 7-slide pitch deck, 30-second video, Python code and a bilingual web app.
details:
What it does and how it works
ALSTRO-Y finds the places on Earth that best match NASA's Moon and Mars targets, so astronauts and rovers can train in realistic conditions. Each Earth site is scored against each target on eight weighted dimensions: water & ice, latitude & light, temperature, dryness, landform, rocks & soil, dust & sand, and living & operations. Three of these dimensions (light, temperature, dryness) are calculated automatically by our Python code from live NASA POWER data. The team rated the other five from published research, and the weights are written down so anyone can check or change them.

Results

  • Shackleton Crater (Moon, south pole) ↔ Haughton Crater, Canada: 66%
  • Jezero Crater (Mars) ↔ Wadi Rum, Jordan: 74%

A cross-check confirms that each Earth site matches its own target best (Haughton–Jezero 52%, Wadi Rum–Shackleton 36%).

Benefits and expected impact

  • Safer, cheaper training: astronauts can practise ice drilling and spacesuit walks at Haughton before going to the Moon.
  • Rovers can test wheels, drills and dust protection in Wadi Rum's Mars-like terrain.
  • A repeatable tool: any new site can be scored the same way in minutes, using free NASA data.
  • Wadi Rum becomes a new hub for training, research and student outreach in Jordan.

Tools, languages and software
Python (requests), the NASA POWER climatology API, the NASA CMR search API, NASA Earthdata (MODIS MOD11A1/MOD11A2, ASTER GDEM), NASA Worldview, NASA Moon Trek, NASA Mars Trek, and the Copernicus Browser (Sentinel-2 NDVI). We built a bilingual web app on Replit with a live NASA backend: https://bilingual-learning-hub.replit.app/

Creativity
Our project turns analog-site selection into a transparent, data-driven score instead of a matter of opinion. It also brings Jordan's Wadi Rum into space exploration as a Mars training site.

Factors we considered
Water ice for permanent polar bases, communication delays (about 1.3 s to the Moon and 3–22 min to Mars), and coarse NASA POWER grid cells. We were also honest about the limits: no place on Earth has low gravity, vacuum or space radiation, and Jezero has no surface ice, so a polar Mars site needs a third Earth analog.
